problem: The sentence 'Every separation operation in a plant is a named way of arranging that push' is false. Many plant separations are mechanical, not mass transfer: filtration, screening, centrifugation, settling of grit in a Chennai water works. A student can carry this line into an exam and call filtration a mass transfer operation.
fix: Say 'Almost every separation that works by moving a component between phases is a named way of arranging that push. Mechanical separations such as filtration and centrifugation are a different family and are not part of this subject.'

problem: The placement and the reason given are muddled. Drying a wet solid with hot air is normally put under phase creation, because heat turns the water into a vapour phase. The clause 'the solid sits still while the air leaves with the water' does not describe a solid agent, which is a solid that takes up solute (adsorption, ion exchange).
fix: Most books place drying with hot gas under phase creation, since heat makes the vapour; a few treat the hot gas as an added phase and put it under phase addition. Drying is never a solid-agent operation in the adsorption sense, because the solid gives up water rather than taking up solute.

problem: Units are missing on a formula that ties two unit systems together, so a student cannot check the factor of 1000 that appears in the worked example.
fix: Write ρA = cA MA with ρA in kg/m³, cA in mol/m³ and MA in kg/mol (divide a molar mass given in g/mol by 1000 first).

problem: 'a flux computed with the wrong one is off by a factor of the molar mass' is loose. Mole fraction and mass fraction are both dimensionless and differ by the ratio of molar masses (times the mean molar mass), and neither can be used as a concentration in a flux formula at all.
fix: Say: mole fraction and mass fraction are dimensionless and are not concentrations; a flux needs mol/m³ or kg/m³. Converting a molar concentration to a mass concentration multiplies by the molar mass in kg/mol.
